# Copper January 2013 - As we enter the new year, there is an air of cautious optimism as global equities rally and as investors become more hopeful about economic prospects. Copper prices continue to benefit from this momentum for now as this market moves into ‘new’ territory with the onset of what looks to be a period of sustained surpluses as production growth is set to outstrip that of demand. - The combination of greater visibility on refined copper production, trade and stock movements in the final months of 2012, coupled with corroborative data on semis production and semis trade flows has led us to marginally downgrade our assessment of world refined consumption last year by ~160kt. The changes are mainly focussed on peripheral consumers with our views on the main consuming nations remaining unchanged. Meanwhile in China, further evidence is emerging to confirm a broader improvement in end use market sectors which is starting to positively impact semis production and capacity utilisation rates across multiple product lines. This bodes well for higher refined copper consumption in 2013. - Spot selling terms between miners and traders were slightly higher than December’s levels, with a representative average of $65/t and 6.5c/lb. After slow progress during November and December, the new year saw a number of negotiations successfully concluded to settle long-term TCRCs for 2013. A rumoured deal between Freeport and Jiangxi Copper effectively established the 2013 benchmark at $70/t & 7.0c/lb. These terms were further supported by another settlement around the same time between Antofagasta’s Esperanza mine and Jiangxi Copper. According to market rumour these deals were swiftly followed by settlements between Freeport and other smelters in China, Japan, India, Philippines and South Korea at the $70/t & 7c/lb mark. Codelco and Anglo Chile are also believed to have fixed terms with Jiangxi Copper at this level, lending further weight to confirming a 2013 benchmark. #### **Copper key forecasts** ||**2011**|**%**|**2012**|**%**|**2013**|**%**|**2014**|**%**| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |**Global (kt)**||||||||| |Total Mine Production|16181|0.0|16799|3.8|17691|5.3|19197|8.5| |Total Smelter Production|15444|4.5|15699|1.6|16611|5.8|17719|6.7| |Refined Production|19738|4.0|20240|2.5|21145|4.5|22584|6.8| |Consumption|19730|2.2|19774|0.2|20769|5.0|21822|5.1| |Concentrate Market Balance|-240||86||50||150|| |Metal Market Balance|8||466||376||761|| |MetalStocks- Days ofCons|57||66||69||78|| |**Prices**||||||||| |Cash LME Price ($/t)|8810||7949||7713||6950|| |(c/lb)|400||361||350||315|| |Contract TC/RCs (c/lb excl pp)|14.2||16.3||17.9||20.7|| |Contract Blister Europe($/t)|85||88||125||135|| _Source: Wood Mackenzie_ Copper Monthly Update ## Market developments As we enter the new year, there is an air of cautious optimism as global equities

rally and as investors become more hopeful about economic prospects. Copper prices continue to benefit from this momentum for now as this market moves into ‘new’ territory with the onset of what looks to be a period of sustained surpluses as production growth is set to outstrip that of demand. 2012 proved to be an erratic year. After the first quarter, economic woes dampened copper’s growth prospects considerably, although prices held their ground against a backdrop of supply disruptions and the dislocation of inventory. The bulk of this inventory ended up in China, with ~750kt+ in bonded warehouses and inventories on the SHFE exceeding ~200kt by the end of the year. As we incorporate news and trade flows to update both production and consumption numbers, we have revised our data for 2012 and the outlook for 2013. It is clear that even with the slew of disruptions that occurred during 2012, meagre global consumption growth of just 0.2% pushed copper into a surplus of ~450kt, pushing stocks out to 66 days of consumption. Our expectations for a surplus in 2013 remains in place, at a slightly higher level of ~370kt, which will push stocks out to 69 days of consumption by the year end. From a fundamental perspective, we would expect prices to yield in the second half as stocks build and further surpluses emerge. **Macro still the main director for copper** Copper prices tailed off over the last week of 2012 as markets slipped in reaction to the chaos that surrounded the last minute resolution to America’s fiscal cliff. Once the deal was finally concluded a rally ensued, with copper hitting a 10-week intraday high of $8255/t in the early days of January. Prices have since scaled back and remain trading in a narrow band of $7900/t to $8150/t. The copper market continues to take direction from the rally in equities and macroeconomic data announcements, with the stronger PMI data out of both the US and China providing support. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

**Labour concerns recede but have not disappeared totally** One of the concerns coming into this year was the potential for disruption from industrial action at several large copper mines. A feature of recent labour negotiations has been early agreements in addition to extended contract periods. Last month we reported that Codelco had reached settlements with workers at its Chuquicamata mine with Escondida the only major settlement outstanding within the Chilean copper mining sector. Workers at Escondida have just voted to approve a new 48-month contract deal. The wage offer is understood to include a 5% raise in salaries, as well a

s a 20M peso (US$42.3k) contract signing bonus which with benefits totals roughly US$48k per worker. The current contracts were due to expire in June this year and workers could have gone on strike sometime in July if negotiations, following a legally-mandated time frame, had fallen through. In contrast Southern Copper’s wage negotiations continue unresolved. Workers in Peru are asking for a 14% wage increase as well as better safety conditions and health benefits. They have agreed to another 15 days of talks in an effort to negotiate a new wage plan. The current contract expired at the end of 2012. There is no question that copper producers must be delighted with prices up at these elevated levels given such uncertain times and the spectre of emerging surpluses. While these higher prices have also benefited the large copper producing economies such as Chile, which accounts for around 40% of that economy’s billion-dollar trade surplus, they have also aided countries such as Zambia that is re-emerging as significant copper player. However, at the producer level the benefits from the surge in prices are less evident. This is because in countries such as Chile, where there has Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2013 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update been a steady appreciation of the Peso against the dollar, copper producers’ incomes have been dented. These escalating labour costs as a result of the last round of negotiations and agreements are cutting further into producers’ earnings at a time when input costs including energy, equipment and consumables, are all continuing to rise significantly, even though general inflation is relatively low. In this environment, currency appreciation translates into lower revenues with this accompanied by increased cost pressures. #### **Currency appreciation dents copper’s rise** 116

As we enter 2013 all eyes are on demand prospects for the largest copper consumer, which continues to import quantities of material even with a negative arbitrage between the SHFE and LME exchanges. Indeed the subdued demand outlook in China in conjunction with the large build in inventory did pose concerns for producers as they began their cathode contract negotiations during the final months of 2012. However it appears that those concerns were unfounded. Companies that we have spoken with have all commented that their buyers, have on balance contracted similar tonnages for 2013 deliveries compared to those agreed for 2012. The difference this year is that less tonnage has been purchased under long-term contracts from traders. It is likely that consumers are keeping their options open, anticipating cheaper buying opportunities (for bot

h prices and premia), if required, in a market poised to register a considerable surplus. The volumes needed by both consumers and traders from the spot market are likely to be more significant this year as both sets of participants may have to rely more on spot business in the absence of long-term contracts in a recovering consumer market and this will lead to far more volatility in spot premia this year. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 800 450

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2013 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update It would seem logical that consumers are opting for the expectation of cheaper buying opportunities ahead, particularly when the consensus outlook for demand growth in 2013 is modest and metals should be readily available. However there are some risks to this particular strategy; material in warehouse may not be easily accessible due to the growing queues that are developing at some locations. We also understand that several suppliers, mainly out of Latin America, are taking up options offered by warehousing companies of $100/t to deliver metal into warehouses. The bulk of this inventory is reported to be accumulating in southern USA. Last month we noted that after a two year wait, JPMorgan had finally received SEC approval for its physically backed copper ETF which could absorb c.62kt of copper if fully subscribed, although the threat of litigation could yet impede JP Morgan’s efforts to launch the fund. Meanwhile, many now also expect the SEC to provide a similar ruling on BlackRock’s proposed copper fund which is due on 22nd February. One further layer of complexity this year comes with the changes to export taxes and export licences in China which means that several of the large Chinese metal producers will be able to export metal. This could lead to destocking of some of the bonded inventories that have built up but only if the arbitrage weighs in favour of exports. **A slow start to 2013** It has been a very slow start to the new year on the demand front and so it comes as no surprise that LME and Shanghai inventories are at 11 and 8 month highs respectively. However, with de-stocking having taken place throughout 2012, this year should see an improvement in demand as fabricators will have no choice but to come into the market, even at these prices, to replenish a supply pipeline that is severely depleted. #### **Copper spot premia – ($/t)** 180 10

Interest in the USA is rather more upbeat and reflects the improving economic outlook, although the US debt ceiling remains an issue. Logistics, in the form of warehouse queues are a concern with consumers understood to have concluded their 2013 long-term contracts quickly in an effort to ensure direct deliveries from the producers. Although spot business is thin, premia are understood to be trading around the 5-6¢/lb level on the East Coast. Thus far with little or no spot business concluded, Europe premia are being quoted just below the long-term contract levels at around $80/t on a CIF Rotterdam basis. Chinese premia had been floating around the $30-35/t mark during the first two weeks of January but have recently improved and are currently being quoted closer to $60-65/t of late. Although there does not appear to be any obvious reason for this uplift, other than a 3.4kt stock decline at SHFE warehouses, it may also reflect some restocking by consumers ahead of the Chinese New Year Holiday in February, or merely a reflection of the overall improvement in sentiment on the back of positive macro data out of the country. This month, the Flash PMI came in at 51.9, beating market consensus, which was at 51.7, reaching a two year high. The market will continue to be supported at current levels, and perhaps higher, for as long as it believes in the China recovery story and/or the on-going lack of supply on account of mine disruptions. As mentioned previously, we have raised our net annual disruption allowance from 5% to 6% to reflect average on-going levels seen in recent years. Thus, having reduced our mine production capability by 1.1Mt for 2013 we still envisage a net production uplift of almost 900kt. And, while the impact of this additional supply will not be immediately evident, we would expect this to feed through to a market reaction with the catalyst being signs that the recovery is derailing, either through ballooning inventories of metal (concentrate, scrap or refined metal) along the chain, or from any meaningful decline in economic activity. Prices should average around $7713/t ($3.50/lb) this year, although we would expect the market to come under pressure in the second half of this year. 2014 will see the surpluses weigh on prices, to average $6950/t ($3.15c/lb). Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

The combination of greater visibility on refined copper production, trade and stock movements in the final months of 2012, coupled with corroborative data on semis production and semis trade flows has led us to marginally downgrade our assessment of world refined consumption last year by ~160kt.  The changes are mainly focussed on peripheral consumers with our views on the main consuming nations remaining unchanged. The exception is South Korea where the release of December data has led us to increase the decline in consumption to 16% last year.  This confirmed that it was truly awful year for the rod business and domestic wire and cable demand.  In Russia, wire rod exports managed to remain at a high tempo supporting local apparent consumption of cathode in 2012 although domestic demand weakened.  Meanwhile in China, further evidence is emerging to confirm a broader improvement in end use market sectors which is starting to positively impact semis production and capacity utilisation rates across multiple product lines. This bodes well for higher refined copper consumption in 2013. 

### **China** 

**Economic outlook begins to brighten** Chinese gross domestic product grew at the slightly faster rate of 7.9% in the fourth quarter bringing growth for the year up to 7.8%.  More encouragingly, industrial production also expanded at the faster rate of 10.3% in the fourth quarter, regaining double digit levels for the first time since the second quarter of 2012. Broader indicators were also supportive with retail sales up 15.2% and fixed asset investment 20.6% higher. Expectations of growth prospects in the first half of 2013 have improved across almost all sectors of the economy from construction to utilities, automotive, home appliances, electronics and also export market opportunities.  The automotive sector remains the most consistent industry performer with December passenger car and commercial vehicle production up by 5.7% and 4.5% year-on-year, respectively.  Total vehicle output in 2012 reached an impressive 19.3M units comprising 15.5M passenger cars (+4.

6%) and 3.75M commercial vehicles (-4.7%).  Vehicle sales grew at almost identical rates, ensuring no noticeable increase in finished vehicle inventories, a problem which was evident through the second and third quarters of the year. 

**Home appliance sector entering restocking phase** Activity at Chinese appliance manufacturers recovered appreciably through November and December as the industry entered a re-stocking cycle after working off the excess unsold stocks of goods that had accumulated through the summer.   Monthly room air conditioner production once again exceeded the 10M unit level in both November and December, rising by 15-17% year-on-year from the depressed levels seen at the end of 2011.  Aside from restocking, an improvement in domestic demand and in export shipments has contributed to the increase.  The swing in momentum has been so swift to have significantly reversed the fortunes of the commercial tube and winding wire suppliers which had experienced falling production and capacity utilisation since May. Output of both product lines is estimated to have increased by as much as 10-15% year-on-year in response to the upsurge in orders from air conditioner manufacturers.  This is likely to keep production at fairly high levels through January and February despite the upcoming Chinese New Year holiday.  Although there are hopes that the sector’s outlook should remain buoyant through the first half of 2013, a sustained improvement will continue to be dependent on a revival in air conditioner exports to rest of the world, and this is by no means certain.  Chinese appliance industry output of household freezers, refrigerators and washing machines has been following the upward trend in air conditioners though at the lower rate of increase of around 5% year-on-year. 

**Interconnect markets are struggling to make headway** Although the recent trends in the automotive and home appliance industries have been mildly supportive, there has still not been a meaningful recovery in the sheet and strip business.  After hitting capacity utilisation levels of 65% in March and April last year, sheet and strip mills saw their production utilisation rates stagnate in the 56-58% range for the remainder of last year.  Electronics markets strengthened towards the end of the year with integrated circuit output surging by 20-25% year-on-year in October and November, but this has brought only a minimal improvement in production volumes.  Although Chinese mills have devoted significant financial investment towards expanding their nameplate capacities, in sheet and strip it has proved much harder to increase commercial production.  The sheet and strip business is less of a commodity market than tube or rod, where Chinese mills have successfully managed to expand their output at the expense of foreign imports of comparable quality.  So except for simple copper and brass alloys for lower technological applications, it is much more difficult for Chinese mills

to successfully and consistently cast complex alloys and to roll the sheet and strip to the tight tolerances required by electrical and electronics OEMs.  Consistent high product quality and service are the main purchasing criteria for consumers.  Price is a secondary consideration, but only so long as the quality standards are met and maintained.  Chinese mills are steadily taking share from imports, but the speed of their advance has been less rapid than expected, especially considering the large volume of commissioned capacity. 

**Construction industry sales and output improving slowly** It is only from November onwards that there has been a meaningful pick up in performance from the construction sector.  The latest indices suggest that commercial and residential construction is reviving measured on a sales area, sales value, investment or new starts basis.  The value of all investment in the property sector increased by a healthy 16.7% to RMB6.5 trillion in the year to November 2012 according to data published by the NBS.  Housing sales rose by 9.1% to RMB 5.4 trillion in the same period, but this only translated into a 2.4% year-on-year increase in the total area of sales to 917 million square metres.  This indicates there is not a huge requirement for a large expansion in the number of residential properties under construction relative to current levels of demand for housing.  Although it is widely anticipated that the pace of both new residential and

commercial construction will increase in 2013 it is not likely to be particularly rapid.  The onset of a cold winter in the Northern provinces will do nothing to spur construction activity or building wire demand in the next couple of months. Realistically it will not be until April or May before a tangible rise in building wire sales might become more discernable across China. 

**Mixed trends in the utilities sector** In 2012 the total value of investment in the power utilities dropped by a modest 1.9% to Yuan 747Bn, reported the China Electricity Council.  Expenditure on power generation facilities fell 3.9% to Yuan 377bn, while spending on the electricity grid rose marginally by 0.2% to Yuan 369Bn.  The main beneficiary of this investment was aluminium which saw a 30% increase in bare overhead conductor shipment tonnage for the transmission network.  Insulated power cable volumes for the distribution network rose by only 12.5% last year, and this is believed to include an increased share of insulated aluminium cables than in 2011 due to an emphasis on rural power grid investment in the first half of 2012.  In the communications sector, copper telecom cable production declined by 13% due to the continuing penetration of fibre optics and wireless technology into the subscriber loop. 

**Semis production likely to be slightly higher in January 2013** The consensus emerging from China is that sem

is output and wire and cable production is expected to be back slightly (+5%) above December’s level in January and that this should also represent a reasonable year-on-year increase (+10-15%) from weak activity levels in January a yearago. This is because the start of the 2012 Chinese New Year fell on 23rd January, but the 2013 New Year will not begin until 10th February. So while fabricators should see a noticeable year-on-year bounce in their January volumes this will be subsequently offset by a year-on-year decrease in their February shipments. It will only be with the arrival of March that a clearer picture of demand will emerge, but with the majority of rod mills having the confidence to raise their production targets for 2013 the balance of opinion is on the upside. 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **South Korea** **Another bad year for Korea** The positive spin on the sharp decline in refined consumption in Korea in 2011 was that at least it should have put a floor under demand to allow a modest recovery last year. However, 2012 proved to be even worse with a precipitous decline in production of cathode intensive semis, despite some improvement in products that use a significant amount of scrap and alloy as their feedstock. For the year as a whole we estimate that consumption fell by 16% to 663kt. **Rod leads Korean woes** Refined copper intensive wire rod led the weakness in semis production with output down by 16% in the January to November period of 2012 and we expect a similar rate of decline for the full year to result in annual wire rod output of around 570kt. The sources of this slump are sliding exports of wire rod and drawn wire in addition to collapsing domestic demand for wire and cable, despite relative strength in exports of wire and cable. Overseas shipments of rod and drawn wire fell to 60kt in 2012 from 91kt the prior year and accounting for 31kt of the c.110kt drop in domestic production. Although Korean rod mills had little success in overseas markets, further downstream, wire and cable makers fared better, with strong export demand for low voltage energy cable and copper power cable, in particular from the Middle East. Given that wire and cable exports increased last year, this suggests truly awful demand for wire and cable in Korea itself. At least some improvement is anticipated in the construction sector this year following the growth in building starts through 2012 which should feed through into better demand for building wire. #### **Korean wire rod production – (kt)** 30 90

**Brassed off with non-cathode intensive semis growth** The brass mill sector overall was more resilient than wire rod although the more cathode intensive products fared the worst. Production of copper tube for example fell by 10.5% in the first eleven months of the year, as commercial tube for the Korean HVACR market suffered the same fate as China. Rod and bar was much better and the stand out sector last year, with output up by 15% year to date, although this failed to lift refined consumption as most of this production will have used scrap as its source feed. Sheet and strip output also expanded through to November, up around 5% year to date, amid reasonable growth in the electronics goods sector, which should continue into 2013 in line with a mild recovery in export markets. **Brighter outlook for 2013** The outlook for 2013 is at least a little better than the past two years. Ind

ustrial production is set to turn higher after slowing sharply last year, with improving economic activity in key export markets helping to drive domestic output of industrial and consumer goods. Many of the key end use sectors are set for strengthening demand, with construction, automotive and electronics set to grow, while Korean cable makers are likely to continue to benefit from contract wins in the healthy Middle Eastern markets. As a result, we anticipate improving exports of semis, wire and cable and end use goods, which will lead to firm growth in refined copper consumption of around 3%. ### **Russia** **Domestic end use demand hits semis production** Following the sharp surge in Russian refined consumption in 2011 possibly the best that could be hoped for in 2012 was a consolidation of previous gains, although domestic semis production failed to maintain the prior year’s level and eased back. This resulted in a contraction in refined consumption of 5% in 2012 to 676kt. **Taxonomy of demand drivers** The reintroduction of a cathode export tax at the start of 2011 resulted in a sharp contraction in overseas shipments of refined copper as Russian cathode producers were incentivised to produce wire rod for export. The economics meant that it was possible for Russian traders to export low quality rod that could be used as cathode at a consumer, thus avoiding the cathode export tax to the benefit of all parties. However, a good deal of the rod exported was used for its primary purpose to be drawn into wire. Given the downturn in neighbouring markets, most notably in Western Europe, a decline in exports seemed likely in 2012 but they actually rose by a modest 1% in the first eleven months of the year. The decline in overall refined consumption set against robust exports of wire rod points to weakness in domestic demand for wire rod and therefore a contraction in wire and cable production and consumption. This trend is also confirmed by the slide in imports of wire and cable, with copper power cable and telecom cable showing the sharpest declines. **Powering down cable demand** In line with the sluggish wire and cable imports data, the power sector would appear to have been a poor performer and we understand that there was a sharp retrenchment in investment from utility companies and this hit power cable output badly. The general weakness in building and construction activity in Russia in 2012 also hampered domestic demand although we forec

ast an improvement in 2013 in line with very tentative signs of recovery.  However, it is unlikely that this will immediately feed through to improved demand for building wire given the lag between starting construction and the installation of internal wiring.  The automotive sector was in fact the beacon of light in an otherwise gloomy backdrop, with production of wiring harnesses mirroring overall double-digit growth of 1015% in motor vehicle production, while further strong sectoral growth is forecast for 2013. 

**Muted growth for 2013** For 2013 overall we forecast only modest growth in Russian refined copper demand of c.1% as the construction sector will still weigh on overall prospects, despite further expansion in automotive production. Moreover, after gaining market share through heavily discounted rod, sold at effectively no margin, we anticipate that increased competition in the European rod market will result in Russia losing at least some market share.  This will need to be offset by improvements in domestic demand, which although forecast, will be sufficient to drive only a muted upturn.

**European Commission proposes stringent new standards for the classification of copper scrap** As a result of a technical report issued by its Joint Research Centre (JRC), the European Commission recommended draft new standards to EU member states on the criteria for identifying copper scrap from waste metal products.  From a technical standpoint the JRC considers that “2% represents a safe environmental limit value on foreign materials for copper scrap to cease to be waste”.  Foreign materials are defined to be other metals, earth, dust, insulation, glass, rubber, plastic, wood or oil.  The European metal trade and recycling federation, Eurometrec, is wholly opposed to the new recommendation on the grounds that it is an unnecessarily stringent restriction on established good business practices. Under the proposed 2% guideline, the vast majority of existing trade in copper scrap would have to be reclassified as waste.  As defined, this would include smelter grade No 2 copper scrap, with a 94-96% copper content, which constitutes most of existing trade flows.  Eurometrec has been actively lobbying for a more appropriate 5% foreign material limit and regards the 2% target as “totally unrealistic”.  It is hoped that further talks will result in a sensible compromise as the EC has said it that it has the latitude to review the criteria if “adverse effects on recycling markets for copper scrap are noted, in particular with regard to the availability of, and access to, such scrap”.  Tighter restrictions on scrap would inevitably increase compliance costs for the supply chain and consumers.

In 2010 measured and indicated resources at Deziwa were stated to total 316Mt at 1.44% Cu and 0.12% Co while the Ecaille C deposit, located 45km from Deziwa, had an inferred resource of 21Mt at 1.15% Cu and 0.06% Co. Gecamines is reported to be considering a $1.5Bn investment in a project to produce 200kt/a of copper from the deposits, although how such a development would be funded remains unclear. **Another Chilean miner considers investment in power generation** Codelco has followed BHP in seeking to address the shortage of electrical power in northern Chile by applying for environmental approval to construct gas fired plants at Mejillones with a total capacity of 780MW. The estimated cost of the project, which is known as Luz Minera is reported to be $758M.
